fields.title: C. T. Studd (For Teens)
fields.description: At twenty-one C. T. Studd was playing cricket for England in the match that gave the world the Ashes. At twenty-four he sailed for China and put on a Chinese gown, and at twenty-six he gave away a fortune. At fifty-two, asthmatic and against medical advice, he went to the north-east of the Belgian Congo, where he spent most of his last eighteen years. This teen edition tells his story straight: the courage and the joy, the money made from Indian labour, the Chinese and Congolese believers who really built the churches, the quarrels, the morphine, the twelve years apart from his wife, and the split in the year he died.

qa.question: Who was C. T. Studd?
qa.answer: An English cricketer, born in 1860, who played for England at the Oval in 1882, went to China in 1885 as one of the Cambridge Seven, and gave away his inheritance. After years in China, America and India he went to the north-eastern Belgian Congo in 1913, founded the mission that became WEC International, and died at Ibambi in 1931.

qa.question: Is the book honest about the hard parts?
qa.answer: Yes. It names the indigo money his family made from Indian labour, the two baby sons who died, his harshness with colleagues, his dismissal of his son-in-law Alfred Buxton, the twelve years he and his wife spent apart, his regular use of morphine for pain, and the split of 1931. It also gives the other side: his real pain, the committee’s real reasons, and the love of the Congolese Christians who buried him.

qa.question: What did he mean by “If Jesus Christ be God and died for me”?
qa.answer: It is the saying traditionally attributed to him: “If Jesus Christ be God and died for me, then no sacrifice can be too great for me to make for Him.” Nobody has traced it to anything he published, but it sums up how he lived. He meant that if Christ had given everything for him, nothing he could give back would be too much.

qa.question: Did C. T. Studd write “Only one life, ’twill soon be past”?
qa.answer: Probably not. He loved the lines and is recorded as sending them to his grandchildren in his last year, but the longer poem built around them says its author first heard them from someone else. This edition treats them as words he loved and lived by, not as his own.

qa.question: How did he treat the people he lived among?
qa.answer: In China he wore Chinese clothes and joined a church Chinese Christians were already leading. In Congo he lived in a local-style house on local food and insisted the Congolese church support its own evangelists. He also called himself Bwana, meaning master, was slow to learn the language, and could be severe with Africans as well as Europeans. Congolese evangelists did most of the preaching that spread the church.

qa.question: Where do the stories come from?
qa.answer: From the full-length Ochorus biography of C. T. Studd, which checks the family accounts against cricket records, the record of the Cambridge Seven, an American’s diary from Niangara in 1914 and modern reference works. Where a story rests only on family tradition, like his last word, this edition says so. There is also a children’s edition for younger readers.

qa.question: What can a teenager today take from his story?
qa.answer: That it is worth giving your whole life to Christ, gladly; that a faith which costs nothing is in danger; that courage without love can wound people; and that you need people who can tell you when you are wrong, and the humility to listen.

qa.question: Why did he and his wife live apart for so long?
qa.answer: From 1916 he led the work in the Congo and Priscilla, whose heart condition kept her from living there, led the mission at home. They loved each other and wrote constantly, but they met only once more, for a short visit in 1928. She died in Spain in January 1929, and he was not with her.

fields.title: The Squire Who Sold His Horses
fields.body_html:
“And they said, Believe on the Lord Jesus, and thou shalt be saved, thou and thy house.” — Acts 16:31 (ASV)

Charles Thomas Studd was born on 2 December 1860 at Spratton, a village near Northampton in England, the third son of Edward and Dora Studd. His family and friends called him Charlie. The world came to know him by his initials: C. T.

The Studds were rich, and it’s worth asking where the money came from. His father had made a fortune as an indigo planter in Bihar, in north-eastern India. Indigo was the blue dye that coloured half the world’s uniforms and work clothes. The work in the fields and the vats was done by Indian peasants, often on terms that kept them in debt and gave them little say over what they planted. In the year Charlie was born, the cultivators of the indigo districts of Bengal rose up against the planters. Charlie grew up on money other people had sweated for. He would spend his adult life giving it away.

In 1871 his father leased Tedworth House, a big country house on the edge of Salisbury Plain, and laid out a racecourse and, for his boys, a cricket ground. He raced horses, and in 1866 his horse Salamander won the Grand National. The family went to church the way people of their class did. Nobody expected it to change anything.

All the Studd boys went to Eton, and Charlie, like his older brothers Kynaston and George, made the cricket eleven. Eton had a religion of the games field that critics nicknamed muscular Christianity: play hard, never complain of pain, never let your side down, never look soft. There was good in it, like courage and loyalty. But it despised weakness and made fear hard to admit. Charlie soaked it up, and some of it never left him.

Then his father changed. Probably in 1875, a friend persuaded Edward Studd to hear D. L. Moody, an American shoe salesman turned evangelist who was drawing huge crowds in London. He went expecting little and came away a new man. He gave up racing, kept a horse for each of his elder sons and sold the rest. He filled the great hall at Tedworth with benches and invited preachers to hold meetings for the neighbourhood. His sons, home from Eton, were embarrassed. When their father asked them in the holidays whether they were saved, they did their best never to be alone with him.

Edward Studd died in July 1877, a Christian for only two or three years. He never saw what came of his prayers.

The next summer a Christian friend of their father’s was staying at Tedworth. The accounts don’t agree on his name, so we won’t guess it. He caught Charlie alone and asked whether he was a Christian. Charlie said he believed in Jesus as much as anyone. The visitor pressed him: did he believe that Christ had died for him, and that God promises eternal life to whoever believes? Then he had it, and he should thank God for it. Charlie saw, as he told it later, that doubting the promise would mean calling God a liar. He knelt and thanked God, and joy and peace came. By family tradition Kynaston and George made the same decision that same day, each without telling the others. Not every account agrees, but by the end of 1878 all three counted themselves Christians.

Paul and Silas told a frightened jailer, “Believe on the Lord Jesus, and thou shalt be saved, thou and thy house.” That isn’t a promise that faith passes automatically from parent to child. The jailer’s family heard and believed for themselves. But God loves to work through families. A father’s prayers opened a door, and his sons walked through it a year after his funeral.

Maybe you’re the embarrassed one, dodging a parent who talks about God too much. Maybe you’re the only one in your house who prays. Either way, prayers don’t stop counting when the person who prayed them is gone.

One thing to do this week: ask an older Christian in your family or church how they came to faith, and who prayed for them. Then pray by name for one person in your own family.

study_questions.answer: A visitor asked whether he believed Christ had died for him and trusted God’s promise of eternal life. He saw that doubting it meant calling God a liar, knelt, and thanked God.

fields.title: Mr Studd at the Oval
fields.body_html:
“Know ye not that they that run in a race run all, but one receiveth the prize? Even so run; that ye may attain. And every man that striveth in the games exerciseth self-control in all things. Now they do it to receive a corruptible crown; but we an incorruptible.” — 1 Corinthians 9:24-25 (ASV)

Charlie had been converted. Then, by his own later account, he went cold for about six years. He never doubted he was saved. He just didn’t let it cost him anything. Jesus described seed that falls among thorns, where “the cares of the world, and the deceitfulness of riches, and the lusts of other things entering in, choke the word, and it becometh unfruitful.” In Charlie’s case the thorns weren’t wicked. They were the pleasant things of a rich young man’s life, and above all, cricket.

He went up to Trinity College, Cambridge, in 1879, and he was no scholar. But he was one of the best cricketers in England. He played for Cambridge from 1880 to 1883 and for Middlesex, and he and his brothers Kynaston and George captained the University side in three seasons running. In first-class cricket he scored 4,391 runs, with eight centuries, and took 444 wickets, most of it in five summers.

The summer of 1882 was his best. A touring team from Australia swept through England, led by Billy Murdoch, with the fast bowler Fred Spofforth, whom the papers nicknamed the Demon. Cambridge was one of the few sides to beat them. Charlie made 118 and 17 not out, and took eight wickets. On 14 August he completed the double, a thousand runs and a hundred wickets in one season. Only the great W. G. Grace had done it before, and the season’s records say Charlie’s hundredth wicket was Grace himself. He was twenty-one.

Then came the Test at the Oval on 28 and 29 August 1882. Spofforth bowled him for nought in the first innings. In the second, England needed only 85 to win, but Spofforth tore through them. For reasons still argued about, the captain held Charlie back until number ten. He went in when the eighth wicket fell, and before he faced a ball the ninth went too. The last man, Ted Peate, swung at Harry Boyle, scored two, and a few balls later was bowled. Australia won by seven runs. Charlie walked off not out, without facing a single ball.

A few days later a London paper printed a mock obituary of English cricket, saying the body would be cremated and the ashes taken to Australia. That joke gave the contest its name. That winter Charlie and George toured Australia with Ivo Bligh’s team, which went to win the Ashes back and did. His Test record was modest, and he never played for England after February 1883.

One detail tells you about his world. When Peate was asked why he hadn’t tried to give the strike to his partner, every version of his answer, in substance, is that he couldn’t trust Mr Studd. Mister. Peate was a professional, older and more experienced. Studd was a gentleman, and gentlemen were called Mister. Charlie grew up being deferred to by poorer, older men and took it as natural. James wrote, “My brethren, hold not the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with respect of persons.” That habit of command would follow him to China and Africa.

Studd never taught that games were sinful. He told young Christians to play and enjoy them with thanks. His complaint against himself was that cricket had taken the place of Christ. Paul didn’t sneer at athletes training months for a crown of leaves. He asked why Christians wouldn’t work as hard for something that lasts.

Think about what gets your best hours: a sport, a game, grades, followers. None of those are wrong. The question is what’s at the centre.

One thing to do this week: track for three days where your best energy goes. Then pick one small, regular thing to give God that same seriousness, like ten minutes of reading or praying before your phone.

study_questions.answer: Not unbelief. He never doubted he was saved, but for about six years he let cricket and comfort crowd Christ to the edge of his life.

fields.title: At George’s Bedside
fields.body_html:
“But when Jesus heard it, he said, This sickness is not unto death, but for the glory of God, that the Son of God may be glorified thereby.” — John 11:4 (ASV)

In November 1883 Charlie’s brother George fell desperately ill. George was the brother closest to him, a fine batsman and his companion on the tour of Australia. For some days the doctors didn’t expect him to live.

Charlie sat by the bed. Years later he described what went through his mind. What was all George’s fame worth now? The runs, the wickets, the newspaper praise, the thousands who had cheered: none of it could help him. The only thing that mattered was whether he was ready to meet God. And Charlie, a Christian for five years, found he was ashamed of how he had lived. He had given cricket his strength and Christ almost nothing.

George recovered, and the family saw it as an answer to prayer. Charlie never forgot the questions he had asked at that bedside.

That winter Moody was preaching in London again. Charlie went, and the preaching that had changed his father brought him back to the joy he had felt at eighteen. This time he didn’t keep it quiet. He started talking to his friends about Christ, invited cricketers to the meetings, and gave away Christian books. Some people found it attractive. Others found it alarming. His family noticed, and not all of them liked it.

Then came the big question: what should he do with his life? He could have become a clergyman, worked among young men at home like Kynaston, or kept playing cricket and talked about Jesus on the side. For some months, by his own account, he didn’t know. He was drawn to teaching about the surrendered life, which said you can’t have a divided heart and peace with God. He took it literally, the way he took everything.

He also heard about the China Inland Mission, founded by Hudson Taylor in 1865. It sent workers far inland, asked them to wear Chinese clothes and live in Chinese houses, and promised no salary: they trusted God for support. To some it looked like madness. To Charlie it looked like the New Testament. In 1884 he met Taylor and offered to go.

His family was dismayed. His mother, a widow for seven years, begged him not to go. Kynaston, a committed Christian himself, thought Charlie was being carried away by emotion. Friends called it a waste. It’s easy to call that worldliness, and Studd’s fans usually do. But these were the fears of a loving family who had already lost a father, and who knew inland China killed missionaries with grim regularity. They weren’t entirely wrong to be afraid.

Charlie said later that their opposition was one of the most painful parts of the decision. He settled it from the Bible and decided he must obey God rather than his family. Jesus warned, “He that loveth father or mother more than me is not worthy of me.” That verse has sometimes been used to excuse cruelty. There’s no sign Charlie was harsh with his family in 1884. He was sorry to grieve them, and he went anyway. Kynaston ended up helping with the preparations.

Notice what Charlie didn’t do. He didn’t say he had never really been a Christian before. When he told the story later, he said he had truly been converted at eighteen. His problem had been a faith that was never allowed to cost anything. That’s more common than unbelief, and maybe more dangerous, because it feels so safe.

Sometimes it takes a hospital bed, a funeral or a scare to show us what matters. Jesus said Lazarus’s sickness was “for the glory of God.” Fame is what people give you. Glory is God being seen. Charlie had had plenty of fame. Now he wanted the other thing.

One thing to do this week: write down one thing you would want to have done if you only had a year left. Then do one small step towards it, and if it involves people who love you, talk it through with them honestly.

study_questions.answer: That fame couldn’t help George at all, and that he himself had given cricket his strength and Christ almost nothing.

fields.title: Seven Young Men
fields.body_html:
“And I heard the voice of the Lord, saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? Then I said, Here am I; send me.” — Isaiah 6:8 (ASV)

By the end of 1884, seven young men had offered themselves to the China Inland Mission, and the newspapers noticed what they had in common. They came from the class that ran Britain. Stanley Smith had stroked the Cambridge boat. Montagu Beauchamp was a baronet’s son. William Cassels was a curate. Arthur and Cecil Polhill-Turner came from a wealthy family, and Cecil was a cavalry officer. Dixon Hoste was an artillery lieutenant and a general’s son. And there was Charlie Studd, England cricketer. Someone called them the Cambridge Seven, and the name stuck.

They weren’t a natural team. Some were Anglicans, some went to newer independent churches. Some were loud, and Hoste was so quiet he was later called the odd one out. What joined them was a choice most people around them couldn’t understand: giving up careers and comfort to live as Chinese people lived, with no salary.

Hudson Taylor saw what their example could do among students. He was also careful. He didn’t want them treated as heroes, and he didn’t change the rules for them. They would sail as ordinary beginners and go where they were sent.

In January and early February 1885 the Seven spoke in universities and cities across England and Scotland. The halls were packed, especially for the two famous athletes. Studd wasn’t a natural speaker. Reports describe him as quiet but intense. He told students that he had loved cricket as much as anyone could, and had found in Christ something far better; that cricket wouldn’t last and honour wouldn’t last, but it was worth living for the world to come. He also told them about his six cold years, and warned that you could be a Christian and still keep Christ out of the centre.

On 4 February 1885 a crowd of about three thousand filled Exeter Hall in London for their farewell, and The Times reported it. The next morning they left for China. A book about them went all over the English-speaking world. In America, Kynaston told the story on college campuses, and at Cornell in January 1886 a student named John R. Mott heard him and later called it a turning point of his life. Mott became the leader of the Student Volunteer Movement, which sent thousands of young Americans and Canadians overseas.

There’s a shadow to this. In the same years the Mission sent out hundreds of others whose names nobody remembers: clerks, shop assistants, nurses, farmers’ sons and servants, many of them women. They wore the same clothes, learned the same hard language, and often died young of the same diseases. Nobody packed a hall for them. Paul wrote that “not many wise after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, are called.” The Seven were celebrated because they were exceptions.

Fame also did something to Studd. From twenty-four he was a public figure whose choices were reported and admired. It isn’t easy to live like that without starting to think your own judgement is especially trustworthy. That would matter later.

Isaiah’s “Here am I; send me” wasn’t the boast of a confident volunteer. It came after he saw God’s holiness and his own uncleanness, and was forgiven. He had nothing left to protect. Their lives went very different ways. Hoste would lead the Mission for over thirty years. Cassels became a bishop in western China. Studd would stay less than ten years. On that February morning, none of them knew. They only knew they had been asked, and had answered.

You may never fill a hall. Most faithful people don’t. God’s work runs mainly on people nobody writes books about.

fields.title: In Chinese Dress
fields.body_html:
“For though I was free from all men, I brought myself under bondage to all, that I might gain the more.” — 1 Corinthians 9:19 (ASV)

The Seven reached Shanghai on 18 March 1885. Shanghai was a treaty port, one of the coastal cities China had been forced to open to foreigners after losing the Opium Wars. It had a foreign settlement with banks, clubs and racecourses. A young English gentleman could have lived very comfortably there. The China Inland Mission existed so that its workers wouldn’t.

Within days they had put on Chinese clothes: a long gown, cloth shoes, and for the men the queue, with the front of the head shaved and the hair at the back grown or lengthened with false hair into a long plait. Many Europeans in China mocked this. They thought it lowered the dignity of the white man. For Hudson Taylor that was exactly the point. His workers were to come as guests and learners, not as members of a ruling race. Studd loved it. He was always more at ease with something that cost him.

There was another reason to come humbly. In the 1880s Britain was the main supplier of opium to China. It was grown under government monopoly in British India and sold in China on terms China had been forced to accept. Millions smoked it, and it wrecked families. Missionaries were told again and again that the nation sending the Bible was also sending the opium. Studd’s own fortune came from a different crop, but from the same empire.

Studd and the Polhill-Turner brothers were sent west by river boat, slow and cramped, and used the weeks to study Chinese. It was hard. Studd learned enough to live and work in it, but he never became a linguist. For the first time in his life he was a beginner. At Eton and Cambridge he had been a star. In China he couldn’t ask for a cup of tea without help, and every child on the street knew more than he did.

Later he moved north to Shanxi province, where millions had died in the famine of 1876 to 1879. Shanxi was also home to one of the most remarkable Christians of the century. Xi Shengmo was a Confucian scholar who had been addicted to opium. He was converted around 1879 by reading the New Testament and broke his addiction through prayer. He took a name meaning conqueror of demons and opened refuges where addicts could be cured with medicine, care and prayer. By the late 1880s Chinese Christians ran them in many towns, and in 1886 Hudson Taylor recognised him as a pastor.

Here’s the key point. The church in Shanxi was already being built by Chinese men and women, often at great cost. The young foreigners in Chinese gowns were joining a work Chinese Christians were leading. Dixon Hoste worked beside Pastor Xi for years and learned a deep respect for Chinese leadership. Studd’s link with him was less close.

From the Mission, Studd took ideas he kept all his life: go to people who haven’t heard, live close to them, trust God for money, lead from the field. What he didn’t take enough of was Taylor’s patience and willingness to listen to others, including Chinese colleagues. Taylor built a mission that could survive him. Studd would build one that nearly didn’t. And in Africa, years later, he arrived as a leader from day one, and never spent long years as a learner among the people he served.

Paul, a free Roman citizen, made himself a servant so nothing about him would get in the way of the gospel. A Chinese gown didn’t make Studd Chinese. But it showed he understood that a messenger who won’t change anything about himself is saying, without meaning to, that his own ways are the gospel.

Being the beginner is uncomfortable. You might feel it in a new school, a new team, or a youth group from another culture. It’s also where you learn to listen.

One thing to do this week: put yourself somewhere you are the beginner: learn ten words of a language a classmate speaks at home, or ask someone from another background to teach you something they know well. Listen more than you talk.

fields.title: Treasure in a Field
fields.body_html:
“The kingdom of heaven is like unto a treasure hidden in the field; which a man found, and hid; and in his joy he goeth and selleth all that he hath, and buyeth that field.” — Matthew 13:44 (ASV)

Under his father’s will, Charlie was to receive his share of the family fortune at twenty-five. He turned twenty-five on 2 December 1885, in China. Legacies take time, and it was around the turn of 1887 before he could do anything with it.

He already knew what he would do. He kept reading what Jesus told a rich young man: “go, sell whatsoever thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come, follow me.” He knew most Christians didn’t take that as addressed to them. He thought it was addressed to him. He was in a mission that asked its workers to trust God for their daily bread. How could he honestly do that with a fortune held in reserve?

The day usually given is 13 January 1887. According to the accounts, he wrote a series of cheques before he even knew the exact size of his inheritance. When he learned the full amount, he gave away most of what was left. The total is reported at between £25,000 and about £29,000. By most reckonings that’s several million pounds today. It was the whole of his own share.

The best-known gifts were about £5,000 each, to four men. One went to D. L. Moody, the evangelist who had reached his father and restored his own faith; it seems to have gone towards Moody’s training work for ordinary Christian workers in Chicago, which grew into the Moody Bible Institute. One went to George Müller of Bristol, who cared for thousands of orphans without ever asking anyone but God for money; Studd asked that most of it go to missions. One went to George Holland, who ran a mission in the slums of Whitechapel in London. And one went to Frederick Booth-Tucker, who had given up a career in the Indian civil service to lead the Salvation Army in India, where its officers lived barefoot among the poor in Indian clothes.

Notice the pattern. Every one of those men lived by faith and among the poor. Two of the gifts went to India, where the family fortune had been made. Whether Studd thought of it as paying something back isn’t recorded. It looks like it.

He kept back about £3,400, which he meant for a future wife. And there’s something he couldn’t give away even if he tried: he was still an English gentleman from a well-connected family that would help him when he was ill and open doors all his life. That doesn’t shrink his gift. But it helps explain why, later, he sometimes failed to understand that people without his background couldn’t live the way he did.

Was it wise? People argued at the time and still do. A fortune invested could have funded mission work for generations. Paul told Timothy to charge the rich to be “ready to distribute, willing to communicate,” which is a command to generosity, not to poverty. But Jesus did sometimes ask particular people for everything. Studd believed he was one of them. It’s hard to prove him wrong.

The saying most often linked with Studd fits this moment, though nobody has traced it to anything he published and its wording varies. It is the saying traditionally attributed to him: “If Jesus Christ be God and died for me, then no sacrifice can be too great for me to make for Him.”

The key words in Jesus’ parable are “in his joy.” The man isn’t making a sacrifice. He’s making the best deal of his life. Every account says that’s how Studd felt. He never spoke of the money with regret. Hold on to that, because later in his story the joy sometimes went missing. Giving away your own fortune gladly is one thing. Demanding that others give, and being angry at their slowness, is another.

One thing to do this week: give something away that actually costs you, money, time or a thing you like, quietly and gladly. Don’t post about it. Afterwards notice whether it felt like loss or like freedom.

fields.title: Scilla
fields.body_html:
“Salute Prisca and Aquila my fellow-workers in Christ Jesus, who for my life laid down their own necks; unto whom not only I give thanks, but also all the churches of the Gentiles” — Romans 16:3-4 (ASV)

Priscilla Livingstone Stewart was born on 28 August 1864, near Belfast; most accounts say in Lisburn. People who knew her described her as warm, quick and full of fun, with a straight-talking Ulster directness. Everyone called her Scilla.

In 1886 Hudson Taylor and his colleagues asked God for a hundred new workers to sail during 1887, without appealing for money. By the end of the year 102 had sailed. Scilla was one of them. Many of the Hundred were young women, and Taylor sent them to live in inland towns, which most missions thought improper and dangerous. He believed Chinese women could best be reached by women, and he trusted them. Scilla was sent with three other young women to a town on the great Poyang Lake. She was a missionary first. She became a wife a year later.

How she and Charlie met isn’t recorded, and later books have decorated the story. He fell deeply in love and pursued her with total conviction. Each of them insisted, with some humour, that the other had proposed. When she fell seriously ill early in 1888, he came to her, though he was getting over a lung illness himself. The Chinese Christians around them thought that settled it: they should marry at once.

They married in the spring of 1888, most accounts say at Tianjin on 7 April. A Chinese pastor performed the ceremony, and they are said to have worn their ordinary Chinese clothes. Some say the pastor was Xi Shengmo, but that can’t be confirmed. An Englishman of his class would normally have married before a consul in English clothes. Their wedding belonged to the Chinese church.

Before the wedding, Charlie gave her the £3,400 he had kept back for her security. She didn’t keep it. She wanted to start married life the way he had, with nothing but God, and she gave the whole sum to the Salvation Army, one of the few Christian movements of the day where women preached and led on equal terms with men. From the start she wasn’t content to be protected. She wanted to share his risks, and she did, for forty years.

They went to Lungan, a city in south-eastern Shanxi now called Changzhi, which didn’t want them. Placards in many places accused missionaries of terrible crimes against children. Some of that came from rumour; some was the resentment of a proud people defeated by foreign powers and forced to accept their merchants, opium and missionaries. The Studds were watched, insulted and threatened. They stayed, lived simply, and saw hostility slowly become tolerance and, here and there, friendship. Their work connected with refuges for opium addicts, very often run by Chinese Christians. Scilla worked among women Charlie could hardly reach. The names of the Chinese believers who worked with them weren’t written down. They still did the riskiest work.

Four daughters were born: Grace in 1889, Dorothy in 1891, Edith in 1892 and Pauline in 1894. Two sons died as babies. The details are uncertain; one record says one lived a day and the other two. Charlie rarely wrote about it, and it would be wrong to invent his feelings. But those small graves were part of the price.

By 1894 both of them had broken health, and Charlie had asthma that never left him. They went home, handing their Lungan property over to the Mission. Six years later, in 1900, the Boxer uprising swept through Shanxi. The China Inland Mission lost fifty-eight missionaries and twenty-one children, and far more Chinese Christians died, many refusing to deny their faith. Missionaries could go home when their health broke. Chinese believers couldn’t.

Paul calls Priscilla and Aquila “fellow-workers.” That’s what Scilla was: not someone’s helper, but a partner with her own call.

One thing to do this week: think of a couple, a pair of friends or a team you know who carry something together. Write them a note naming what each one brings, not just the one people usually notice.

study_questions.answer: She gave all £3,400 to the Salvation Army, so that they would start married life depending on God alone.

study_questions.question: Why is it important that she came to China before she married?
study_questions.answer: She was a missionary with her own call and gifts, one of the Hundred, not just a missionary’s wife.

study_questions.question: Who carried the greatest risk for the church in Shanxi?
study_questions.answer: Chinese Christians. They ran refuges, worked with foreigners at their own risk, and in 1900 many died for their faith, while missionaries could go home.

fields.title: Why Not Go Himself?
fields.body_html:
“How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher? and how shall they preach, except they be sent?” — Romans 10:14-15 (ASV)

The Studds came home in 1894 with four small daughters, poor health and no money of their own. Charlie was thirty-three: a famous cricketer at twenty-one, a famous missionary at twenty-four, and now a semi-invalid with asthma and no obvious work. They lived simply, with help from relatives and friends, and by the standards of the poor they were still very fortunate.

With no adventure to carry him, he didn’t sink into self-pity or try to get his money back. In 1896 and 1897 he spent about eighteen months speaking on American campuses for the Student Volunteer Movement. From 1900 to 1906 he was pastor of the Union Church at Ootacamund, a hill town in southern India where British officials and soldiers escaped the heat. His work there was among the British who ruled India, not among Indian people. The family was together, and the girls grew up with their father at home. He was faithful in work with no drama.

But he was restless. He had come to believe that the world’s greatest need was for the gospel to reach people who had never heard it at all. Ootacamund already had churches. In 1906, ill again, he brought the family home.

In 1908, walking in Liverpool, he saw a notice outside a hall, worded in the sensational, insulting way missionary posters of the time often talked about Africans. Inside, a German missionary named Karl Kumm was speaking about the peoples of central Africa who had never heard the gospel, and the traders, hunters and slavers reaching them first. Studd came out with a question he couldn’t shake. Why had no Christians gone? Because no one had been sent. And then the personal question: why shouldn’t he go himself?

He had every reason not to. He was forty-seven, asthmatic, with a history of serious illness. He had no money, no mission behind him, and a wife in poor health who didn’t want him to go. He went against medical advice. To him it was simple obedience. He was right that God sometimes calls people to do what common sense forbids. He wasn’t always willing to consider that common sense might sometimes be God speaking too.

At the end of 1910 he sailed for the southern Sudan to see for himself. He became convinced that in the north-east of the Belgian Congo lay a large region with no Protestant mission. There were Catholic missions in parts of it, but like most British evangelicals then, he didn’t count them. On the voyage he also became convinced his call was to the whole unreached world.

Back in England, he applied to the Africa Inland Mission in November 1912 and was accepted. fields.title: Bwana at Niangara
fields.body_html:
“For we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus as Lord, and ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake.” — 2 Corinthians 4:5 (ASV)

Studd sailed early in 1913, most accounts say on 30 January. He was fifty-two. With him went Alfred Buxton, about twenty-one, from a great evangelical family descended from the man who led the fight in Parliament against slavery in the British Empire. Alfred had been preparing for a medical career and gave it up to go. He was in many ways Studd’s opposite: patient, gentle, quick at languages. For more than ten years he would be Studd’s closest partner.

They went by sea to East Africa, then by railway, steamer and on foot through what are now Kenya and Uganda to Lake Albert, and across into the Belgian Congo. The journey took about nine months. They reached Niangara, a government post on the Uele River, on 16 October 1913. The church that grew from their work still remembers the date, and celebrated a hundred years in 2013.

You can’t understand this place without knowing what had just happened there. From 1885 to 1908 the Congo had been the personal property of King Leopold II of Belgium. His regime forced people to collect wild rubber and ivory. Villages that missed their quotas were burned, people were beaten, mutilated and killed, and millions died through violence, famine and disease. An international protest, with Protestant missionaries among its leaders, forced Belgium to take over in 1908. In the north-east the Azande and Mangbetu kingdoms had resisted conquest for years. Slavers from the north had raided long before. The people of the Uele had every reason to be wary of white men who arrived uninvited.

For the first year we have an unusual witness. An American named Hayes Perkins worked at Niangara in 1914 and kept a diary. He didn’t share all of Studd’s views, and he could be unfair. But he was there, and he wasn’t writing for supporters.

Perkins noted that Studd announced his African name would be Bwana, a Swahili word for master, and pointed out with some irritation that it wasn’t even used in Bangala, the local trade language. White men across the region were called that. But it isn’t a title Jesus would have taken. The man who had worn a Chinese gown in Shanxi slipped back into the role of the white master. Perkins also noted that it was Buxton, not Studd, who preached to people in Bangala. Studd hadn’t learned it yet.

Another entry stands out. When Perkins was left in charge, the first thing he did was tell the mission’s workers they no longer had to attend morning and evening prayers. It isn’t clear how the rule had been enforced, and Perkins may have overstated it. But if people who depended on the mission for wages had to come to prayers, they weren’t choosing the gospel. Perkins was right that faith has to be freely chosen.

And the people of the Uele did choose. They decided whether to work for the mission, whether to come and listen, and whether to believe. Many came out of curiosity and left unconvinced. Some came back. In time, Congolese men and women were baptised and became evangelists themselves. Their choices, not the missionaries’ plans, decided whether there would be a church.

On 19 August 1914 a telegram brought news of war in Europe. Most of the African troops at Niangara were sent to the front. Tens of thousands of Congolese men were conscripted as soldiers and porters for the campaigns in East Africa, and very many died far from home. The missionaries’ accounts say little about that. Late in 1914 word came that Scilla was seriously ill, and Studd left the work with Buxton and went home.

Paul said, “we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus as Lord, and ourselves as your servants.” You can give away a fortune and still expect to be in charge.

One thing to do this week: notice one place where you expect to be treated as the boss, at home, in a group chat, on a team. Do one thing there that serves instead of directs.

study_questions.answer: Studd called himself Bwana, meaning master, and it was Buxton, not Studd, who preached in Bangala.

fields.title: The Chocolate Soldier
fields.body_html:
“Suffer hardship with me, as a good soldier of Christ Jesus. No soldier on service entangleth himself in the affairs of this life; that he may please him who enrolled him as a soldier.” — 2 Timothy 2:3-4 (ASV)

Studd came home early in 1915 to a country at war. Hundreds of thousands of young men had volunteered, cheered through the streets, and men who didn’t go were often treated with contempt. Scilla recovered. Studd threw himself into meetings, calling Christians to give themselves to reaching the world as completely as soldiers were giving themselves to the war.

His best-known writing came out of these years: a short, angry tract called The Chocolate Soldier. A chocolate soldier was a toy that melts as soon as it gets hot, and Studd used it for Christians who look like soldiers of Christ but melt at the first touch of hardship. The tract declares that heroism is the lost chord of Christianity. It compares the church, unfavourably, with airmen, polar explorers and the volunteers of the war, and argues that if Christians had their pluck, everyone on earth could hear of Jesus within ten years. It ends by asking each reader whether he will be a shirker or a fighter for Christ.

There’s real power in that. Christians who admire a soldier’s courage often expect to follow Jesus without any courage at all. Paul used the same picture: “Suffer hardship with me, as a good soldier.”

There’s also something troubling, and readers a century later feel it more. Millions of young men died in that war, some shamed into volunteering. The tract praises their courage with no hint of the horror, and borrows the recruiting sergeant’s contempt for shirkers to recruit for Christ. Many of the Christians it scolds had families to feed and debts to pay, and no fortune behind them, not even one given away. The tract has no word for them.

Studd had another voice. In 1915 he wrote Christ’s Etceteras, a pamphlet that became the seed of his mission’s rules. In it he described his band as the humblest of helpers, Christ’s etceteras, going to places no one else reached, not to compete but to fill the gaps. It’s one of the gentlest things he wrote. When he thought about his own mission, he could be modest. When he thought about the church at large, he could only shout. Later the shout grew louder, and it landed on his own colleagues.

The meetings found recruits, some of them working men and women the older missions would never have taken. They were brave, many were very able, and some served for decades. Others found the life he demanded more than they could bear. Studd called people to heroism and offered them hardship. The people who answered were not the kind to be easily told what to do, and Studd expected to be obeyed. It was an explosive mix.

In 1916 he sailed again for the Congo with his daughter Edith and a party of recruits. Scilla stayed to run the mission at home. Studd was fifty-five. So far as the record shows, he never saw England again. He and Scilla would meet only once more, for a few days.

Back in the Congo he lived in a house built in the local way, ate local food, and worked far into the night, rarely taking a day off. His colleagues found it exhausting, and some found it frightening. He had little patience with illness or rest in others, though he was constantly ill himself. Edith married Alfred Buxton in the Congo in 1917. In 1920 his youngest, Pauline, came out with her husband Norman Grubb. Their baby son Noel died on his first birthday and was buried at Nala.

A good soldier of Christ serves a Saviour who “came not to be ministered unto, but to minister.” The chocolate soldiers in the tract were real. So were the ordinary, scared, slow Christians Jesus also loves.

One thing to do this week: think of someone you’ve quietly judged as weak or lazy. Ask them one honest question about what their life is like right now, and listen to the answer without fixing it.

study_questions.question: What is a chocolate soldier, in Studd’s tract?
study_questions.answer: A toy that melts in the heat: a Christian who looks like a soldier of Christ but gives way at the first hardship.

study_questions.question: What is troubling about the tract?
study_questions.answer: It uses the shame of wartime recruiting to recruit for Christ, praises the war without its horror, and shows no understanding for ordinary people with families and debts.

study_questions.answer: It was humble, describing his mission as small helpers filling the gaps. It became the seed of the mission’s rules.

fields.title: The Church in the Forest
fields.body_html:
“For from you hath sounded forth the word of the Lord, not only in Macedonia and Achaia, but in every place your faith to God-ward is gone forth; so that we need not to speak anything.” — 1 Thessalonians 1:8 (ASV)

Around 1921 or 1922 Studd moved his base to Ibambi, in the forest country to the south. He lived there for the rest of his life. Most of what’s been written about his mission shows Congolese people only as crowds, converts and carriers. That isn’t because they didn’t matter. It’s because they didn’t write the books. This chapter tries to tell it the other way round, as far as the sources allow.

Around Ibambi lived the Budu, a farming people whose villages were scattered through the Ituri forest. To the north and east were the Mangbetu and Azande, with their own kingdoms. In the forest lived the Mbuti hunters, with long traditions of their own. They had their own beliefs about God and the spirits, their own elders and ways of settling disputes, and a deep knowledge of the forest. Their world had already been turned upside down by slave raids, the Congo Free State and now Belgian rule.

Life under the colony was hard: a head tax payable in money, forced labour on roads, compulsory cotton, and state gold mines that drew in workers recruited under heavy pressure. A man who walked days to hear the gospel might have to leave the next week to work on a road. So when people heard that God loved them, that the poor and despised were welcome in his kingdom, and that one day every wrong would be judged, many heard it as good news for themselves, not as a European message.

Most people didn’t first hear it from a missionary. When Studd died, his mission had only about thirty or thirty-five European workers spread over a huge area. People heard from a relative, a neighbour, a fellow worker, or an evangelist from their own people. From early on, Congolese evangelists went out to villages with no church. They taught people to read, led worship and gathered small congregations. They walked narrow forest paths, depended on villages with no reason to welcome them, and sometimes faced hostile chiefs or officials. In time some churches sent out their own evangelists at their own cost. One later report speaks of a single congregation in Budu country supporting fifty, though it may describe the years after Studd.

According to the mission’s own accounts, Studd insisted the Congolese church pay its own evangelists, not rely on European money. In a poor country under colonial tax, that put a real weight on poor believers. But it also meant the evangelists belonged to the Congolese church. They weren’t white men’s employees. They were the church’s own messengers.

The gospel spread in people’s own languages. Norman Grubb helped translate the New Testament into Bangala. With two colleagues, Stapleton and Lowder, Studd began a translation into Kingwana, the Swahili of the region, and Luke and Acts were published in 1930. No foreigner translates the Bible alone. Congolese speakers explained words and corrected mistakes. Their names weren’t recorded. They were translators too.

Believing cost something. Converts had to give up many village customs, and missions didn’t always separate what was against the gospel from what was merely unfamiliar to Europeans. Some said no, or came for a while and left, or joined the Catholic mission. Those were real choices too, and they deserve respect.

And there was Studd himself. A modern Christian reference work says plainly that his conflicts were with Africans as well as with missionaries and family. The details aren’t recorded. The Congolese church learned the gospel from him, and it also learned to survive his severity.

It lasted. After independence in 1960 came war, and in 1964 the Simba rebellion swept through the area. The church didn’t disappear. Today it is CECCA 16, centred at Isiro, led by Congolese Christians, with between about 120,000 and 250,000 people in its community. Paul told the Thessalonians the word had “sounded forth” from them, not from him.

One thing to do this week: ask someone who came to faith outside your own culture or country how the gospel reached them, and who brought it. Thank God by name for the people in their story.

study_questions.question: Who did most of the preaching that spread the church in the forest?
study_questions.answer: Congolese evangelists and believers, who walked to distant villages, often supported by their own churches.

study_questions.question: Why did Studd want the Congolese church to pay its own evangelists?
study_questions.answer: So they would belong to the Congolese church, not be employees of the mission. It was also a real burden on poor Christians under colonial tax.

study_questions.question: What does it mean that the church learned to survive his severity?
study_questions.answer: Studd’s harshness reached Africans too, yet the Congolese church kept the gospel and grew, and still lasts as CECCA 16.

fields.title: A Sharp Contention
fields.body_html:
“And there arose a sharp contention, so that they parted asunder one from the other, and Barnabas took Mark with him, and sailed away unto Cyprus” — Acts 15:39 (ASV)

In 1919 the mission took a new name at home, the Worldwide Evangelisation Crusade, because Studd believed his task was the whole unreached world. Workers soon went to Brazil, and later to Arabia and India. The mission now known as WEC International had begun. But the 1920s were also the years when it was torn apart, and much of the conflict centred on Studd. Every honest account has to face this, and the evidence comes mainly from people who loved him.

Studd demanded total commitment. He expected his missionaries to live on very little, work very long hours, and put the work before health, family and comfort, as he did. He treated caution as unbelief and disagreement as disloyalty. He could be warm, generous and funny, and many loved him. He could also be suspicious, harsh and unjust, and he wrote letters that wounded deeply. Some missionaries resigned. Others were dismissed. One letter from 1925 admired his sacrifices and at the same time described him as domineering. That mix runs through almost every account.

The saddest parting was with Alfred Buxton. Alfred had gone with him in 1913, held the work together when Studd was away, learned the languages and married Edith. When conflicts grew, he couldn’t simply take his father-in-law’s side; he thought some criticisms were fair and said so. In 1927 he went to America to repair damaged friendships. Studd called it disloyalty and dismissed him. One account says the dismissal included Edith. Alfred had done nothing worse than disagree and try to make peace. It does Studd no credit.

There is another side. The two men’s bond was never broken; they went on loving each other through the quarrel. Alfred didn’t turn bitter. He went on to open new work in Ethiopia, and he was killed in London in 1940 when a bomb struck a committee meeting.

Why was a man so devoted so hard on others? He was ill, in pain and exhausted for most of his last fifteen years. He lived far from his wife and from any equal who could speak frankly to him. He had grown up expecting leaders to command, not consult. And he believed so completely that no sacrifice was too great that anyone who held back looked like they were failing Christ. None of that excuses him. It helps you understand him.

His marriage was strained by distance too. When he sailed in 1916 they had been married twenty-eight years, and they didn’t see each other again for twelve. They weren’t estranged. They wrote constantly, and every account says they loved each other to the end. Paul told married couples not to live apart except “by consent for a season.” A season isn’t twelve years. It cost Scilla her husband’s company through illness and heavy work. It cost him the one person who knew him well enough to tell him the truth and be heard.

In 1928 Scilla, in her sixties and with a heart condition, made the long, dangerous journey to the Congo. It was her only visit, and a short one; one account says thirteen days. It was the last time they saw each other. On 15 January 1929 she died at Málaga, in Spain, aged sixty-four. He was not with her. He lost his partner, his defender at home, and the person who had made his work possible.

Paul and Barnabas split over John Mark, and Luke doesn’t say who was right. Years later Paul asked for Mark, “for he is useful to me for ministering.” The man he had refused became a man he needed. The Bible doesn’t hide its heroes’ quarrels, and God’s work went on through them. That doesn’t make quarrels good. It means God isn’t defeated by them.

Disagreeing with someone you love isn’t betrayal. Sometimes it’s the most loyal thing you can do.

One thing to do this week: if there’s someone you’ve fallen out with over a disagreement, send a short message that doesn’t argue the point again but says the relationship still matters to you.

fields.title: Hallelujah
fields.body_html:
“For I am already being offered, and the time of my departure is come. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith” — 2 Timothy 4:6-7 (ASV)

By the late 1920s Studd’s body was failing. He had asthma, years of tropical illness, and gallstones that caused attacks of intense pain. No surgery was available anywhere near Ibambi. According to Norman Grubb, a doctor passing through recommended morphine, and Studd, who wanted above all to keep working, agreed. In his last years he took it regularly.

His family never hid it. To critics it was a scandal: the leader of a mission demanding total self-denial, taking a narcotic every day, with supplies that some said were brought in without being declared. Some called him an addict. To his defenders it was medicine, the standard treatment for severe pain then, taken to keep working, not to escape. Here’s what can fairly be said. Anyone who takes morphine for a long time becomes physically dependent; that’s how it works, and it isn’t a moral failure. Whether it affected his moods and judgement can’t be known, though it may have. His pain was real. And the Congolese around him had far less medicine for pain at least as great. Paul says to restore people “in a spirit of gentleness; looking to thyself.”

Meanwhile the committee in London was alarmed. They had heard about the quarrels, the dismissals and the morphine. A 1928 booklet with a deliberately shocking title had offended many supporters. After Scilla’s death nobody held the two sides together. In 1930 and 1931 the committee moved to remove Studd as leader. Grubb and another son-in-law, Colonel David Munro, took the mission’s records so control stayed with those loyal to Studd; Grubb said he had the legal right as Studd’s chosen successor. Thirty-six missionaries left and formed a new mission. Was the committee wrong? Not simply. They were responsible for the mission and its workers, and it’s hard to see what else they could have done. It’s also hard to see how Studd could have accepted it. The proverb says, “in the multitude of counsellors there is safety.” Studd had led all his life and never learned to be led.

In his last year he wrote to his grandchildren and included two lines he loved but did not write. The longer poem built around them says its author heard them from someone else: “Only one life, ’twill soon be past, Only what’s done for Christ will last.”

He died at Ibambi on 16 July 1931, aged seventy. Those with him, or who heard from them, said his last word was “Hallelujah,” which means praise the Lord. Nothing else records it, but there’s no reason to doubt it.

A huge crowd of Congolese Christians came to bury him, many from far away; the accounts say more than a thousand, perhaps two thousand. That matters. He had quarrelled with his committee, his missionaries and his family. But the people he had come to serve, who had known his severity, had also known his love, and they honoured him. He lies at Ibambi among them.

WEC nearly died with him. Grubb, a gentler, patient leader, rebuilt it, and by 1965 it had grown from about thirty missionaries to some eight hundred in twenty countries. The forest church kept growing, through revival and through war.

There are two easy ways to remember Studd: only the hero, or only the problem. Both are wrong. He took Jesus’ words with complete seriousness and gave everything. He also let his zeal outrun his love and couldn’t bear to be told he was wrong. Both are true. Neither cancels the other.

Paul didn’t claim to be perfect. He claimed to have finished and kept the faith. Studd stumbled and hurt people, but he didn’t turn back or stop trusting Christ. You have one life too. The question is how to give it to Christ with his courage and more love than he managed.

One thing to do this week: write those two lines Studd loved on a card. Under them, write one way you want to give your life to Christ, and one person you need to love better while you do it.

study_questions.question: How does this book judge Studd’s use of morphine?
study_questions.answer: Fairly: he took it for real, severe pain, never hid it, and long use brings physical dependence that isn’t a moral failure. It may have affected his temper, but that can’t be known.

study_questions.question: Was the London committee simply wrong to try to remove him?
study_questions.answer: No. They had real reasons and real responsibility. But Studd, who had never learned to be led, could not accept it, and the mission split.

study_questions.question: What does his funeral show?
study_questions.answer: That the Congolese Christians he served, who had known his severity, also knew his love and came in great numbers to honour him.
